title: Electric flux and Gauss's law: choosing the right surface
voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 11
OpenStax: Electric flux and Gauss-law equations

chapters.title: Flux uses the normal, not the surface plane
chapters.formula: Phi = E A cos(theta) for a flat area in a uniform field; units N m^2/C
points: The area vector is perpendicular to the surface.
Theta is the angle between the field and the area normal.
Flux is signed and measures the field's normal component integrated over area.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Imagine holding a flat frame in a breeze. Face it into the breeze and plenty of air crosses its opening. Turn it edge-on and much less crosses. Electric flux uses a similar geometric idea, although electric field is not a flowing substance. For a flat surface in a uniform field, flux equals field magnitude times area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the area vector. The area vector points perpendicular to the surface. That angle is not automatically the angle to the plane of the surface. If a question gives the angle to the plane, convert it to the angle to the normal. Let's take a field of two hundred newtons per coulomb and area zero point zero three square meters. If the field makes sixty degrees with the chosen normal, flux is three newton square meters per coulomb. At ninety degrees to the normal, the field lies along the plane and flux is zero. Reversing the normal reverses the sign. For a curved surface or varying field, split the area into tiny patches and add the field dot area contributions, which becomes a surface integral. An open surface has a chosen normal convention. A closed surface uses outward normals. Flux is a scalar, but its sign carries the direction of the field through that oriented surface.

chapters.title: Closed-surface flux counts enclosed charge
chapters.formula: Closed integral E dot dA = Qenclosed/epsilon0; epsilon0 approximately 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2/(N m^2)
points: Gauss's law relates total outward flux to net charge inside a closed surface.
The field in the integral includes contributions from inside and outside charges.
Zero net flux does not imply zero field at every point.
chapters.script: Now close the surface completely, like an imaginary box around a region. Gauss's law says its total outward electric flux equals the net enclosed charge divided by vacuum permittivity. Add enclosed charges algebraically. An outside charge does not contribute to the net enclosed charge, even though its field can be strong on the surface. In the flux integral, the electric field is the total field from all sources. For an external source, field entering and leaving makes zero net closed-surface flux. This is the trap to remember: zero enclosed charge means zero net flux, not necessarily zero field. Put an empty box in a uniform field. Field passes through it; flux entering one side cancels flux leaving the other. Let's enclose plus two nanocoulombs and minus half a nanocoulomb. Net charge is one point five nanocoulombs. Divide by eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, giving about one hundred and sixty nine point five newton square meters per coulomb. Move an outside charge around and this total stays the same, provided no charge crosses the boundary. But individual surface fields change. Gauss's law applies to any closed surface. To turn it into a simple formula for field strength, however, we need enough symmetry to know the field direction and how its magnitude varies over our chosen surface. The law and the shortcut are not the same thing.

chapters.title: Spherical symmetry and a charged shell
chapters.formula: E outside = kQ/r^2; E inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell = 0
points: Choose a concentric spherical Gaussian surface for a spherically symmetric distribution.
The radial field has constant magnitude on that surface, so flux is E times 4 pi r^2.
Uniform thin-shell results differ from those of a uniformly volume-charged solid sphere.
chapters.script: Consider an isolated thin spherical shell with charge distributed uniformly over its surface. Symmetry tells us that field must be radial, with the same magnitude everywhere at a fixed distance from the center. Choose a concentric imaginary sphere of radius r. The field is along its normal, so the flux becomes field times four pi r squared. Outside the shell, the enclosed charge is the entire shell charge. Gauss's law gives the same outside field as a point charge at the center. Inside the shell, enclosed charge is zero. Because the spherical symmetry still makes the field constant and radial on a concentric sphere, the field is zero. This last conclusion uses symmetry, not zero flux alone. For shell charge two nanocoulombs and shell radius ten centimeters, at twenty centimeters from the center the field is four hundred and fifty newtons per coulomb, using the Coulomb constant nine times ten to the ninth. At five centimeters inside, the field is zero. These results assume an isolated, uniformly charged thin shell. Don't substitute them for a solid insulating sphere with charge spread throughout its volume. For that different model, enclosed charge inside grows as r cubed, and field grows linearly with r. Nor should you assume an arbitrary shell remains uniformly charged when external sources distort its distribution. Always name the distribution before choosing the surface.

chapters.title: A long line needs a cylinder
chapters.formula: E = lambda/(2 pi epsilon0 r) for an ideal infinite uniformly charged line
points: The field is radial around the line and constant on a coaxial cylindrical side.
The side contributes flux; the flat end caps contribute zero.
Real finite-line approximations need points far from the ends.
chapters.script: For an ideal infinitely long uniformly charged straight line, a sphere is an awkward choice. A coaxial cylinder matches the symmetry. Let the cylinder have radius r and length ell. Field points radially away from a positive line and has constant magnitude on the curved side. On the flat end caps, field lies along the surface rather than through it, so their flux is zero. The side contributes field times two pi r ell. Enclosed charge is linear charge density lambda times ell. Substitute into Gauss's law and the cylinder length cancels. Field is lambda divided by two pi epsilon zero r. Unlike a point charge, this field falls as one over r, not one over r squared. Let's use lambda equal to two nanocoulombs per meter and r equal to ten centimeters. With k equal to nine times ten to the ninth, the equivalent relation two k lambda divided by r gives three hundred and sixty newtons per coulomb. Double r and the field becomes one hundred and eighty, not ninety. The imaginary cylinder is a calculation surface; it is not a physical conducting tube. For a finite charged wire, the infinite-line approximation is most useful near its central region when perpendicular distance is much smaller than the distance to either end. Without that approximate symmetry, the end-cap argument and simple formula cannot be used blindly.

chapters.title: A large sheet and the factor of two
chapters.formula: Infinite nonconducting sheet: E = sigma/(2 epsilon0); conductor just outside: E = sigma_local/epsilon0
points: A symmetric sheet uses a pillbox with equal flux through both faces.
Field is independent of distance in the ideal infinite-sheet model.
A conducting surface differs because the field inside its material is zero in electrostatic equilibrium.
chapters.script: For an ideal infinite nonconducting sheet with uniform surface charge density, symmetry gives equal field magnitudes on both sides, perpendicular to the sheet. Choose a short imaginary pillbox crossing it. No field crosses the curved side. Both flat faces contribute outward flux, so the total is two E A. The charge inside is sigma times A, and field becomes sigma divided by twice vacuum permittivity. That factor of two is easy to lose. If sigma is one point seven seven times ten to the minus nine coulombs per square meter and epsilon zero is eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, field magnitude is one hundred newtons per coulomb on either side. It does not decrease with distance in this infinite-sheet model. A finite sheet needs distances small compared with its lateral size and points away from edges for this approximation. Now contrast a conducting surface in electrostatic equilibrium. Field within the conducting material is zero. A tiny pillbox straddling its surface gets flux only through the outside face, giving the field just outside as local surface charge density divided by epsilon zero. Here sigma means the charge density on that particular conductor face, not automatically the total charge divided by both faces of a slab. Our closing routine is simple: identify symmetry, choose a closed surface, write every flux contribution, count enclosed charge, and only then solve for the field.

quiz.question: A flat area of 0.03 m squared has uniform E = 200 N/C at 60 degrees to its chosen normal. Flux is:
quiz.explanation: Phi = EA cos(60 degrees) = 200 x 0.03 x 0.5 = 3.

quiz.question: A closed surface encloses +2 nanoC and -0.5 nanoC. Using epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12, net outward flux is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Net enclosed charge is 1.5 nanoC, so flux is 1.5 x 10^-9 / (8.85 x 10^-12) = 169.49.

quiz.question: An isolated uniformly charged thin spherical shell has Q = 2 nanoC and radius 0.10 m. At r = 0.20 m, using k = 9 x 10^9, E is:
quiz.explanation: Outside the shell E = kQ/r squared = 18/0.04 = 450 N/C.

quiz.question: An ideal infinite line has lambda = 2 nanoC/m. At r = 0.10 m, using k = 9 x 10^9, field magnitude is:
An infinite uniform nonconducting sheet has sigma = 1.77 x 10^-9 C/m squared. Using epsilon0 = 8.85 x 10^-12, field magnitude on either side is:
quiz.explanation: E = sigma/(2 epsilon0) = 100 N/C. This is not the one-face conductor formula.

quiz.question: A closed surface has zero enclosed charge. What necessarily follows?
options: Electric field is zero everywhere on it
Net electric flux through it is zero
Every surface patch has zero flux
quiz.explanation: Gauss's law fixes the total flux. Nonzero entering and leaving contributions may cancel.
